journal_name: Journal of Visual Communication and Image Representation

abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a fundamental rethinking of image representation theory based on visual attention-driven information selection. Traditional image representation paradigms treat all image regions as equally important during encoding and decoding processes, which fundamentally misaligns with human visual perception mechanisms. We propose the Perceptual Saliency Maximization (PSM) framework, which establishes a unified theoretical foundation connecting bottom-up visual attention, foveal sampling strategies, and rate-distortion optimization. The core innovation lies in reformulating image representation as a dynamic resource allocation problem where encoding complexity is adaptively distributed according to region-level perceptual importance scores derived from multi-scale feature analysis. We mathematically prove that under the new framework, optimal image representation must satisfy the condition of marginal perceptual utility equality across all selected sampling locations. Experimental validation on standard benchmarks demonstrates that the PSM framework achieves 40% bitrate reduction compared to conventional approaches while maintaining equivalent perceptual quality as assessed by subjective viewing tests. This work establishes a new paradigm for visual communication systems design by shifting the theoretical focus from pixel-level accuracy to perceptually-optimized information delivery. The proposed framework provides essential theoretical guidance for next-generation image coding standards and multimedia communication protocols.

This paper presents a substantial theoretical advancement in video coding by extending the classical rate-distortion theory to incorporate temporal visual masking effects. Conventional video compression frameworks rely on spatial and temporal just-noticeable-difference (JND) models that treat visual masking as static, ignoring the dynamic interaction between motion perception and texture sensitivity. We derive a unified mathematical framework that characterizes the temporal visibility threshold as a function of both frame difference magnitude and motion trajectory characteristics. The proposed Temporal Visual Masking (TVM) model establishes that perceptual redundancy in video sequences follows a non-linear relationship with motion coherence, leading to significantly higher compressibility in regions exhibiting structured motion patterns. We prove that optimal quantization in the TVM framework requires adaptive deadzone adjustment proportional to local motion entropy. Experimental results on multiple video test sequences demonstrate that incorporating the TVM model into existing hybrid video coding architecture achieves 15-22% bitrate savings while preserving equivalent subjective quality. The theoretical contribution lies in providing a rigorous analytical foundation for temporal perceptual quantization that can be seamlessly integrated into contemporary video coding standards including emerging Versatile Video Coding (VVC) frameworks.

We present a novel end-to-end image compression system that fundamentally departs from traditional block-based coding architectures. The proposed Neural Foveal Codec (NFC) implements a biologically-inspired representation mechanism that simulates foveal vision processing through hierarchical attention-driven sampling. Unlike conventional approaches that apply uniform processing across entire images, NFC employs a learned sampling policy that dynamically allocates encoding resources to perceptually salient regions while progressively discarding redundant background information. The system architecture consists of three integrated components: a perception-guided region proposal network that identifies high-importance image areas, a variable-resolution encoding module that maintains high fidelity in foveal regions while efficiently representing peripheral information, and a learned synthesis decoder that reconstructs images from the hierarchical representation. The training procedure optimizes a perceptual quality metric that balances reconstruction accuracy with compression efficiency. Comprehensive evaluation on high-resolution photographic and medical imaging datasets demonstrates that NFC achieves superior rate-perceptual quality tradeoffs compared to both traditional JPEG2000 and learning-based methods. The system demonstrates particular advantages for visual communication applications where bandwidth constraints require aggressive compression while preserving essential visual information. This work introduces a new paradigm for image coding system design based on perceptually-motivated neural architectures.

This paper presents a significantly enhanced video quality assessment and optimization system that integrates deep learning-based quality modeling into the video processing pipeline. While existing video processing frameworks optimize for objective metrics such as PSNR or SSIM, they often fail to capture perceived quality degradations introduced by compression artifacts and transmission errors. We design the Perceptual Quality-Aware Video Processing (PQAVP) system, which incorporates a learned perceptual quality predictor as a differentiable optimization objective during video encoding and enhancement. The system introduces three key architectural innovations: a multi-scale temporal quality feature extractor that captures both spatial artifacts and temporal discontinuities, a quality-guided rate allocation module that dynamically distributes bits across frames based on perceptual importance, and an adaptive enhancement network that selectively applies restoration to low-quality regions. The quality predictor is trained on a large-scale subjectively-annotated video quality database to ensure alignment with human perception. Experimental results on standard video quality databases demonstrate that PQAVP achieves average improvements of 18% in VMAF scores and 25% in subjective quality ratings compared to conventional rate control strategies. The proposed system provides a practical solution for improving visual experience in bandwidth-constrained multimedia communication applications while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for real-time deployment.
